t.3.63.1: Though he was the elder brother, Rāghava, who grasped the essence of things, accepted the well-spoken words of deep substance as soon as Lakṣmaṇa had uttered them.
t.3.63.2: Restraining the anger that had swelled within him, the mighty-armed Rāma, leaning upon his splendid bow, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.63.3: What shall we two do, dear child, or where shall we go, Lakṣmaṇa? By what means might I see Sītā? Think this over.
t.3.63.4: To Rāma, who was thus tormented by anguish, Lakṣmaṇa said: "You should search this very Janasthāna."
t.3.63.6: And various dreadful caves, teeming with herds of many kinds of beasts, and the dwellings of the Kiṃnaras, and the abodes of the Gandharvas.
t.3.63.5: It is strewn with many rākṣasas and filled with many kinds of trees and creepers; here there are mountain fastnesses, clefts and caves.
t.3.63.8: "In times of misfortune they do not tremble, just as mountains do not tremble before the force of the winds." Thus addressed, he wandered through that entire forest together with Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.63.7: Together with me, you ought to search through all those places, for men like you, O bull among men, are endowed with wisdom and are great-souled.
t.3.63.10: He saw Jaṭāyuṣa fallen on the ground, drenched with blood; seeing him, who looked like a mountain peak, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa: "By this one Sītā Vaidehī has been devoured, there is no doubt about it."
t.3.63.9: Then the enraged Rāma, fitting a terrible razor-edged arrow to his bow, turned upon that illustrious best of birds, who looked like a mountain peak.
t.3.63.11: Clearly this is a rākṣasa in the form of a vulture roaming the forest; having devoured the large-eyed Sītā, he sits here at his ease. I shall slay him with terrible, straight-flying arrows whose tips are blazing.
t.3.63.12: Having spoken thus, the enraged Rāma fitted a razor-edged arrow to his bow and rushed at the vulture, as though shaking the earth bounded by the ocean.
t.3.63.13: Then the bird, vomiting foaming blood, addressed him, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, in a most piteous voice.
t.3.63.14: O long-lived one, the lady whom you seek in this great forest like a healing herb, and my life-breaths as well, both have been carried off by Rāvaṇa.
t.3.63.15: O Rāghava, I saw the queen, left alone without you and Lakṣmaṇa, being carried off by the mighty Rāvaṇa.
t.3.63.16: I rushed to Sītā's aid, and in the battle Rāvaṇa, his chariot and parasol shattered, was struck down by me onto the surface of the earth.
t.3.63.18: When I was utterly exhausted, Rāvaṇa cut off my wings with his sword, seized Sītā, the princess of Videha, and flew up into the sky. I have already been struck down by the rākṣasa; you should not kill me.
t.3.63.17: This is his broken bow, and this is his quiver; and here, O Rāma, is his war chariot, shattered in battle.
t.3.63.19: Rāma, having understood his dear tale concerning Sītā, embraced the king of vultures and wept together with Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.63.21: Fall from the kingdom, dwelling in the forest, Sītā lost, the bird slain: such is this misfortune of mine that it could burn up even fire itself.
t.3.63.20: Seeing him alone in that narrow, impassable place, barely breathing, the grieving Rāma spoke these words to Saumitri.
t.3.63.22: Even if I were to cross the great ocean today, brimming full though it is, surely that lord of rivers too would dry up through my ill fortune.
t.3.63.23: There is no one more unfortunate than I in this world of moving and unmoving beings, since I have fallen into this great snare of calamity.
t.3.63.24: This king of vultures, my father's friend, burdened with old age, lies struck down upon the ground because of the reversal of my fortune.
t.3.63.25: Having spoken thus many times, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, touched Jaṭāyus, showing him the affection due to a father.
t.3.63.26: Rāma embraced that king of vultures, his wings cut off and drenched in blood, and crying out, "O Maithilī, dear to me as my very life, where are you?" he fell to the ground.
